question: LOKI_SIMPLE=1 cuts the assembled prompt 78%. That is a TOKEN measurement. Does the stripped arm still build the thing, and does it take more or fewer iterations?
method: benchmarks/run-prompt-ablation.sh, 5 trials per arm. ONE engine copy, same spec, model (sonnet), caps and machine -- the arms differ by a single environment variable read at prompt-assembly time. The engine stamps prompt_arm from its OWN environment and the harness refuses to record a trial whose stamp disagrees with the harness label. Acceptance is an artifact check (greet.js_exists), not a self-report.

result.acceptance: 5/5 in BOTH arms -- no regression from stripping the prompt
result.act_iterations: 1 in every run of both arms -- no change

the_n3_trap: AT n=3 THIS DATASET LOOKED LIKE AN 18% SPEEDUP WITH PERFECT SEPARATION. The first three simple trials were 415, 419, 450s against full's 462, 493, 532s -- every simple run beat every full run. The design floor at n=3/3 is p=0.1, so the analyser reported UNDERPOWERED and no claim was published. Trials 4 and 5 came in at 506 and 1330s and the separation vanished entirely: p rose to 0.5714 with a floor of 0.0079, meaning the test had ample power and found nothing. Had the floor been ignored at n=3, this repository would have shipped a false 18% speed claim.
actual_finding: CORRECTED. An earlier revision of this file claimed the stripped arm was '9.6x more variable'. That was an artifact of a NON-ROBUST statistic. Testing dispersion three ways by exact permutation on the same n=5/5 data: range p=0.4048, stdev p=0.0952, MAD p=0.8016. None is significant, and the robust one is decisive -- median absolute deviation is 31s (full) vs 35s (simple), essentially identical. The 915s spread rests entirely on ONE 1330s run; permuting labels relocates that single point freely, which is why range and stdev inflate while MAD does not. There is ONE slow simple run and no measured variance effect.
verdict: SAFE ON OUTCOMES. NO SPEED EFFECT. NO VARIANCE EFFECT MEASURED. LOKI_SIMPLE=1 completed 5/5 in one iteration each, identical to the full prompt. Wall clock p=0.5714 (floor 0.0079). Dispersion not significant by range, stdev or MAD. The honest summary at n=5/5 is that stripping 78% of the prompt changed nothing measurable on this spec except producing one slow outlier. SCOPE: one trivial spec, 1 iteration per run -- see scope_limit. This does not license shipping LOKI_SIMPLE=1 as a default on real work.
not_claimed: No multiplier is reported. The 78% prompt reduction is a TOKEN measurement and says nothing about outcomes; only the acceptance and iteration results below speak to behaviour. Arms differ by one environment variable in one binary on one machine -- nothing here compares Loki to another vendor.
two_traps_this_dataset_contained: A LOCATION TRAP at n=3: perfect separation (simple 415/419/450 vs full 462/493/532) that looked like an 18% speedup. The exact-permutation floor at n=3/3 is 0.1, so no claim was published; trials 4-5 (506, 1330s) collapsed it to p=0.5714.
A DISPERSION TRAP at n=5: a 9.6x range difference that looked like a real variance effect. Range and stdev are outlier-driven; MAD shows 31s vs 35s with p=0.8016. One run, not a property of the arm.
scope_limit: ONE SPEC, AND A TRIVIAL ONE. Every trial built the same task: a Node CLI that prints 'Hello, <name>!' (benchmarks/speed-benchmark.sh:62-67), completed in ONE act_iteration by both arms. A prompt that coaches planning, decomposition and gate recovery has little to do on a task that needs none of those, so this result CANNOT be generalised to real specs. It says LOKI_SIMPLE=1 is safe here, not that it is safe. The sharper experiment is the same ablation on benchmarks/bench/fixtures/hard-1-order-api or hard-2-ledger, which is not a quick run: those fixtures ship a README only, and run-prompt-ablation.sh hardcodes the greet spec (it does not plumb speed-benchmark.sh's --spec through), so it needs a written spec plus a harness flag before any trial can start.
